mcq.q: You switch embedding models with the same dimensions. You must…
options: Re-embed the corpus and switch query encoder and index together
mcq.why: Different models produce incompatible vector spaces even at equal dimensions.

mcq.q: Why can you not compare a query embedded with model B against documents embedded with model A?
options: They live in different vector spaces
mcq.why: Scores can look normal while results are random.
distractors: Even equal dimensions do not make them compatible.

mcq.q: Why should queries reach an index through an alias such as kb-search?
options: So switching indexes is an atomic alias change, not a code change
mcq.why: Rollback is then switching the alias back.

mcq.q: How is the new index backfilled when only the embedding model changes?
options: From stored chunk text, without re-parsing, at a throttled rate
mcq.why: Re-parsing is needed only if the chunker or parser changed.

mcq.q: What does dual-writing during a migration do?
options: Writes twice to the same index
Sends every new change to both old and new indexes so the new one does not fall behind
mcq.why: The backfill and live changes both reach v4.

mcq.q: What must happen before cutting over to the new index?
options: Offline evaluation showing it meets the gates
mcq.why: Then shadow or canary reads.

mcq.q: At cut-over, what must switch at the same moment as the alias?
mcq.why: Otherwise queries are embedded for the wrong space.

mcq.q: Why keep the old index warm after cut-over?
options: So rollback is just switching the alias back during the rollback window
mcq.why: For example, two weeks.

mcq.q: What is the peak extra cost of a blue/green index migration?
options: About double storage during the overlap
mcq.why: Budget for it in capacity plans.

mcq.q: What should an index manifest record?
options: Embedding model and version, dimensions, normalisation, chunker, parser and ANN parameters
mcq.why: A query service can refuse an index whose embedder differs from its own.

interview.q: Why is changing the embedding model a migration, not a config change?
Walk through a blue/green index migration.
covers: Switch alias with the query encoder; keep v3 warm

interview.q: What is an index manifest, and what does it prevent?
covers: Records model, chunker, parser and ANN settings

interview.q: You switched embedding models and recall dropped. How do you roll back safely?
interview.followUp: What would you change in the process so this is caught before cut-over?

interview.q: Estimate the cost and duration of re-embedding 65 million chunks.
{company} is moving to a multilingual embedding model. Plan the migration.
Design a migration framework your team can reuse for any index change.
How would you migrate when the chunker changes too?
covers: Re-parse or re-chunk from stored text

mcq.q: A stale queued update overwrote a newer document. The fix is…
mcq.why: Write only if the incoming version is newer than the stored one.

mcq.q: How are incremental updates usually detected?
options: Change feeds, webhooks, delta APIs, database CDC or periodic hash diffs
mcq.why: Only what changed is processed.

mcq.q: How should a changed document's chunks be replaced?
options: Append new chunks and keep the old
Atomically: the new version appears and the old disappears in one step
Edit chunks in place one by one
mcq.why: Queries should never see both versions, or neither.

mcq.q: A source document is deleted. What must also be removed?
options: Its chunks, cached answers and any derived summaries
mcq.why: Deletion speed can be a legal requirement (16.5).

mcq.q: Many connectors miss deletes. What catches them?
options: Periodic reconciliation: list all IDs at the source and diff with the index
mcq.why: Reconciliation repairs what missed events left stale.

mcq.q: When deduplicating copies of a file across sites, what must you remember?
options: All locations, because each copy may have different permissions
mcq.why: Keep one canonical chunk set, with the permission sets of every copy.

mcq.q: Which fields belong in a chunk's lineage?
options: Source system, document ID, version, parser version, chunker config, embedding model version, timestamps
mcq.why: Lineage answers “why did the assistant say this?” and “what must be rebuilt?”.

mcq.q: How is a freshness guarantee measured?
options: By indexed_at − source_modified_at for each change
mcq.why: For example, 99% of edits searchable within 10 minutes.

mcq.q: Unchanged chunks of an edited document have the same content hash. What can you do?
options: Reuse their existing vectors to save embedding cost
mcq.why: Only changed chunks need new vectors.

mcq.q: Five changes had lags of 2, 3, 4, 5 and 30 minutes. The target is 99% within 10 minutes. Is it met?
mcq.why: Freshness is a percentile target, not an average.
distractors: One of five missed the target.

interview.q: How do you keep a RAG index fresh as documents change?
What must happen when a document is deleted?
What is lineage, and what questions does it answer?
A user says the assistant quoted a policy that was deleted last week. Investigate.
covers: Check the index for the document
interview.followUp: What alert would have caught it?

interview.q: Design a freshness SLO and how you would measure it.
covers: Percentile targets for edits and deletes

interview.q: {company} removes listings and changes prices constantly. Design freshness for {assistant}.
Design deletion handling that meets a legal deadline across index, caches and summaries.
How would you use lineage to recover from a parser bug?
covers: Find chunks with the bad parser version

mcq.q: One tenant has 70% of traffic and lives on one shard. Best mitigation?
options: Dedicated shards/replicas sized for that tenant
mcq.why: Isolate and scale the hot tenant's own capacity.

mcq.q: What is the difference between a shard and a replica?
options: A shard is a subset of the index; a replica is a copy of a shard on another node
A replica is a subset; a shard is a copy
mcq.why: Shards scale data and writes; replicas scale reads and availability.

mcq.q: What is scatter-gather?
options: Queries fan out to the relevant shards and results are merged
mcq.why: Hash placement makes every query touch every shard.

mcq.q: What is the trade-off of placing documents by tenant?
options: Queries touch few shards and isolation is good, but shard sizes can be very uneven
mcq.why: Hash placement spreads load evenly but fans out every query.

mcq.q: What is a hot tenant?
options: One tenant with far more data or traffic, overloading its shard
mcq.why: A noisy neighbour (15.5).

mcq.q: How much memory headroom does the topic suggest for index rebuilds?
mcq.why: Rebuilds and growth need space.

mcq.q: Ingestion is the bottleneck. A team adds replicas. What happens?
options: Little: replicas help reads, not writes
mcq.why: Writes go to every replica, so replicas can even add write work.
distractors: Replicas do not add write capacity.

mcq.q: When should a shard be split?
options: Before it exceeds what a node can rebuild quickly after a failure
mcq.why: Long rebuilds extend the time at reduced redundancy.

mcq.q: A platform has 12,000 tenants and gives the 50 largest dedicated collections. How many share the common shards?
In the mixed strategy, when is a tenant promoted to dedicated shards?
options: When it passes about 5M chunks or 50 QPS
mcq.why: Thresholds based on size and traffic.

interview.q: Explain shards, replicas and partitioning strategies.
What is a hot tenant, and how do you handle one?
What goes into capacity planning for a vector index?
One tenant suddenly has 70% of traffic on a shared shard. What do you do now, and later?
covers: Short term: rate limit or add replicas
interview.followUp: How would you move the tenant without downtime?

interview.q: Hash placement or tenant placement for 12,000 tenants? Argue it.
{company}'s largest sellers dominate traffic before sales. Design shard placement and replicas.
Design an index topology for a multi-tenant SaaS assistant.
How would you plan re-sharding for a growing index?
covers: Triggers by size and rebuild time

mcq.q: 10 million documents × 6 pages × 500 tokens per page is how many tokens?
distractors: Three orders of magnitude too few.

mcq.q: 30 billion tokens in 512-token chunks with 10% overlap gives about how many chunks?
mcq.why: Each chunk adds about 461 new tokens: 3 × 10¹⁰ ÷ 461 ≈ 65 million.

mcq.q: 65 million 768-dimension float32 vectors take about how much space?
The same vectors in int8 take about how much?
mcq.why: int8 is a quarter of float32.

mcq.q: HNSW links at about 128 bytes per vector add how much for 65 million vectors?
distractors: That confuses bytes per vector with GB.

mcq.q: int8 vectors (50 GB) plus links (8 GB), with 2 replicas, need about how much RAM across the cluster?
mcq.why: (50 + 8) × 2 = 116 GB, before metadata and rebuild headroom.

mcq.q: Embedding about 33 billion chunk tokens once at an illustrative $0.02 per million tokens costs about…
mcq.why: 3.3 × 10⁴ million tokens × $0.02 ≈ $660–670, repeated on every embedding-model change.

mcq.q: Why measure sizing assumptions on a sample of your real corpus?
options: Each assumption changes the result several-fold
mcq.why: Pages, tokens, chunk size, overlap, dimensions, precision and replicas all multiply.

mcq.q: A plan counts only raw vector bytes as the RAM requirement. What is missing?
options: Graph links, metadata, replicas and rebuild headroom
mcq.why: Total memory is several times the raw vectors.

mcq.q: What repeats the full embedding cost?
mcq.why: Every vector must be recomputed (10.7).
distractors: Replicas copy vectors, not recompute them.

interview.q: Walk through sizing a RAG corpus from documents to RAM.
Which sizing assumptions matter most, and how do you check them?
Why does an embedding-model change matter for cost?
Estimate the RAM for 10 million documents at 768 dimensions with int8 and 2 replicas.
covers: About 50 GB int8 plus 8 GB links
interview.followUp: How does the answer change at 1,536 dimensions?

interview.q: Your vector database runs out of memory despite the plan. What did the plan probably miss?
Size {company}'s index for listings plus reviews, and plan for a future embedding change.
covers: Listings and reviews as separate collections

interview.q: Design a capacity plan for a corpus that grows 30% a year.
{company} retains case notes for years. How does retention change your sizing and design?

mcq.q: What does a durable queue between ingestion stages provide?
options: Decoupling, so each stage can scale and fail independently
mcq.why: Producers and consumers no longer need to run at the same speed.

mcq.q: What is a checkpoint in ingestion?
options: A durable record of progress, so a crashed job resumes instead of restarting
mcq.why: For example, a connector's last sync cursor.

mcq.q: What is backpressure?
options: Slowing upstream stages when downstream is slower, instead of overflowing
mcq.why: Bounded queues and consumer-paced pulling implement it.
distractors: More queues do not slow producers.

mcq.q: What is a dead-letter queue for?
options: Items that exceeded retry limits, so they do not block the pipeline
mcq.why: Monitor and replay it.

mcq.q: Why derive chunk IDs from document ID + version + position?
options: So reprocessing the same item gives the same result (idempotent upserts)
mcq.why: At-least-once delivery then produces no duplicates.

mcq.q: An old version's job finishes after a newer one. What prevents it from overwriting fresh content?
options: A version guard: write only if the incoming version is newer (compare-and-set)
mcq.why: Queues redeliver and reorder.

mcq.q: When should a worker acknowledge a message?
options: As soon as it is received
After its result is durably committed, or after a recoverable outbox record exists
mcq.why: Early acknowledgement loses work on a crash.
distractors: A crash would lose the work.

mcq.q: 4 workers process 20 documents per second each, and 100 documents arrive per second. How fast does the queue grow?
mcq.why: Capacity is 80/s, so 20/s accumulate.

mcq.q: Worker latency looks fine, but the oldest message in the queue keeps getting older. What is happening?
options: A freshness incident: work is backing up
mcq.why: Watch queue age, not just worker speed.

mcq.q: A parser crashed after writing chunks but before acknowledging. What happens on redelivery if chunk IDs are deterministic?
options: The writes are repeated as upserts, so no duplicates appear
mcq.why: Idempotency makes at-least-once delivery safe.

interview.q: Design an ingestion pipeline for millions of documents.
What is backpressure, and why does ingestion need it?
Why must index writes be idempotent and version-guarded?
Your queue's oldest message is two hours old. Walk through your response.
interview.followUp: What would you alert on so this is caught earlier?

interview.q: How do you handle poison documents that crash the parser?
{company}'s sellers push price updates in bursts. Design ingestion so an old price never wins.
Design checkpointing and replay for a connector that syncs from a source system.
{company}'s pipeline must never index text that failed PII scrubbing. Design the controls.

mcq.q: Why are PDFs hard to extract text from?
options: They describe pages: text can be positioned glyphs with no reading order, columns and headers mixed in
mcq.why: Layout analysis is needed to recover reading order.

mcq.q: What does a scanned document need that a born-digital PDF does not?
mcq.why: Scanned pages are images with no text layer.

mcq.q: Why record OCR confidence per page?
options: So low-confidence pages can go to review or a better model
mcq.why: Poor scans produce unreliable text.

mcq.q: How should tables be stored for retrieval?
options: Extracted as rows and columns, then as Markdown or row-as-sentence chunks, with the original kept for display
mcq.why: Flattening loses which number belongs to which column.

mcq.q: How should images and diagrams be indexed?
options: Caption with a vision-language model, OCR any text in them, index those and link back to the image
mcq.why: Multimodal embeddings can also index images directly.

mcq.q: Why preserve headings, list numbering and page numbers as metadata?
options: They improve chunking, filtering and citations
mcq.why: For example, “Policy 4.2, page 17”.

mcq.q: Per-diem answers are wrong because a region-by-limit table was flattened to text. What fixes it?
options: Store the table as structured rows
mcq.why: Row-as-sentence chunks keep each value with its row and column.
distractors: The model never sees the structure.

mcq.q: A parse produced a lot of text. Can you assume it was read correctly?
options: No: run a quality gate for garbled text, near-empty pages and low OCR confidence
mcq.why: Volume is not correctness.

mcq.q: Which are signals a parse quality gate should check? Choose all that apply.
options: A high rate of non-dictionary words
mcq.why: Flag or reject such outputs for review.
distractors: Authorship says nothing about parse quality.

mcq.q: Why route scanned pages to a separate OCR pool?
options: OCR has different, heavier compute needs, often GPU, with its own capacity
mcq.why: Separate pools keep heavy work from blocking normal parsing.

interview.q: Why are PDFs hard to parse, and what tools help?
covers: Layout analysis tools such as PyMuPDF, pdfplumber, Docling

interview.q: How should tables be indexed for RAG?
What does a document parsing pipeline look like?
Answers about prices from a pricing table are often wrong. How do you investigate?
interview.followUp: What test would you add so the fix stays fixed?

interview.q: How would you handle a corpus where 30% of documents are scanned?
{company} receives scanned statements and forms. Design the parsing and review flow.
Design a parsing service that can be improved without breaking answers.
How would you index diagrams and images so their content is searchable?

mcq.q: Where must access control be enforced in a RAG system?
options: In retrieval, before content reaches the prompt
mcq.why: The model sees whatever is retrieved.
distractors: Too late: the model has seen it.

mcq.q: What is early binding?
options: Checking each result with the source API after retrieval
Storing each chunk's allowed principals as metadata and filtering by the user's groups inside the search
mcq.why: Fast, but correctness depends on keeping ACLs in sync.

mcq.q: What is late binding?
options: Checking each candidate against the source system's permission API after retrieval
mcq.why: Always current, but slower; over-fetch to keep enough results.

mcq.q: What is common practice for permissions?
options: Early binding for filtering, a late check for high-sensitivity sources, short sync intervals and immediate updates on change events
mcq.why: Combine speed with currency.

mcq.q: Where should the tenant ID for a query come from?
options: The server, from the authenticated session, as a mandatory filter
mcq.why: Never from the prompt or model output (16.4).

mcq.q: An ACL for a document is unknown. What should retrieval do?
mcq.why: Fail closed.

mcq.q: Why keep an urgent deny list?
options: Index ACL sync always lags; the deny list blocks revoked users, groups or documents immediately
mcq.why: It is checked against the authoritative source on every query.

mcq.q: What must cache keys include so a revocation also invalidates cached answers?
options: The user's access scope and the policy version
mcq.why: Otherwise a cached answer keeps serving revoked content.
distractors: Users with different access would share answers.

mcq.q: The system prompt says “don't reveal restricted documents”. Is that access control?
options: No: the model can be manipulated and has already seen the content
Yes, if the prompt is long
mcq.why: Enforce access before generation.

mcq.q: A user loses access at minute 5; ACLs sync every 30 minutes; there is no deny list or late check. When does access really end?
options: At the next sync, up to 30 minutes later
mcq.why: The deny list or a late check closes that window.
distractors: Not without a deny list or late check.

interview.q: Explain early and late binding for permission-aware retrieval.
covers: Early: ACL metadata filtered in search
Late: source API check after retrieval

interview.q: How do you guarantee tenant isolation in retrieval?
Why is a prompt instruction not access control?
covers: Model has already seen the content

interview.q: A user who left Finance can still get Finance answers for 30 minutes. Fix it.
interview.followUp: How would you test that the fix works?

interview.q: Design cache keys for a permission-aware assistant.
{company}'s staff assistant must show only cases assigned to the agent. Design enforcement and revocation.
covers: Filter by team and assignment in search

interview.q: Design ACL synchronisation from an identity provider for nested groups.
How would you test permission-aware retrieval continuously?
covers: Probe cases per tenant and role

mcq.q: Why are vendor benchmarks a poor guide to production?
options: They use clean public data, single tenants, no filters and no writes
mcq.why: Your benchmark must reproduce your conditions.

mcq.q: How do selective permission filters affect ANN search?
options: They remove the need for ANN
They can change latency and recall a lot compared with no filter
mcq.why: A user who sees 2% of the corpus behaves very differently.

mcq.q: Why run the benchmark while updates stream in?
options: Heavy writes can hurt latency and recall in HNSW graphs and segment merges
mcq.why: Production indexes receive writes continuously.

mcq.q: Which measures should a retrieval benchmark report together?
options: Recall versus exact search, Recall@k versus labels, latency percentiles at target QPS, resources and cost
mcq.why: Trade-offs are only visible together.

mcq.q: Why benchmark at 10%, 30% and 100% of the target corpus?
options: To see the trend instead of extrapolating from a tiny sample
mcq.why: Behaviour changes with scale.

mcq.q: A benchmark repeats the same queries many times. What does it mostly measure?
mcq.why: Use varied queries sampled from logs.
distractors: Cached results are faster than real ones.

mcq.q: In the topic's example, reaching 0.95 recall costs about 10 ms clean but about 25 ms with selective filters. What should you plan with?
mcq.why: Only the realistic condition predicts production.

mcq.q: The laptop ANN lab uses random vectors. How does that affect recall?
options: Recall is pessimistic, because random vectors have no cluster structure
mcq.why: It still teaches the efSearch curve and memory behaviour.

mcq.q: Which cost figure should a retrieval benchmark report?
mcq.why: It converts infrastructure into a comparable unit.

mcq.q: A team benchmarks on a 1% sample and extrapolates linearly to 100%. What is the risk?
options: Behaviour such as memory and latency may not scale linearly
mcq.why: Measure at several scale steps.

interview.q: What makes a retrieval benchmark realistic?
Which metrics should a retrieval benchmark report?
covers: Resources and cost per million queries

interview.q: Why do selective filters matter for ANN performance?
Design a benchmark before choosing a vector database.
interview.followUp: What result would disqualify a candidate?

interview.q: Your benchmark looked great, but production latency is three times worse. What did it miss?
Design {company}'s search benchmark for festival conditions.
How would you run continuous retrieval benchmarks as part of releases?
Explain to a vendor why their benchmark numbers do not apply to you.

mcq.q: When should you adopt an advanced retrieval technique?
options: When evaluation shows the failure pattern is common and the technique fixes it better than simpler fixes
mcq.why: Simpler fixes first: parsing, hybrid search, reranking, query rewriting.

mcq.q: What does hierarchical search do?
options: Indexes summaries at document and section level as well as chunks, searching coarse first
mcq.why: It helps big-picture questions over very large corpora.

mcq.q: How does late interaction (ColBERT) score a document?
options: One vector per token; sum over query tokens of the maximum similarity to any document token (MaxSim)
mcq.why: Fine-grained matching that a single vector blurs.

mcq.q: A 2-token query: token 1's best document-token similarity is 0.9, token 2's is 0.6. What is the MaxSim score?
What is the main cost of late interaction?
options: 10–100× more vectors per chunk and specialised indexes
mcq.why: Compression and indexes such as PLAID reduce it.

mcq.q: Which questions do knowledge graphs (GraphRAG) help with most?
options: Multi-hop relationship questions and corpus-wide themes
mcq.why: Extraction is expensive and must be kept fresh.

mcq.q: What does agentic retrieval do?
options: An agent chooses indexes or tools, rewrites queries, judges results and iterates
mcq.why: More LLM calls per question, higher latency and variance.

mcq.q: Only 6% of queries were multi-hop, and query decomposition fixed most of them. What should the team do about a knowledge graph?
mcq.why: The evidence does not justify the cost.

mcq.q: A user asks “Which merchant category had the most fraud this month?”. What is the right tool?
options: A SQL or dataframe query over structured data
mcq.why: Aggregates need exact computation, not a few retrieved chunks.

mcq.q: A team adopts GraphRAG because it is popular. What is missing?
options: A failure analysis showing the gap it would fix
mcq.why: Adopt by evidence, not by name.

covers: Route to SQL or analytics tools

covers: Pick by measured gain per cost
